speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals):	I move that the
preliminary statement of accounts of the Canadian National Railways for the year 1927, laid on the table of the house on Tuesday, March 6, be referred to the select standing committee on railways and shipping.
Mr. C. IL. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):	It is usual, on the motion of the
Minister of Railways to refer these accounts to the committee, to have a presentation by the minister to the house of the financial affairs of the Canadian National Railways. It is impossible for members of the 'house to have access to the typewritten statement that has been presented, and it seems to me that another occasion should be afforded, after the printed return is brought down and distributed, for hon. members to make themselves thoroughly acquainted with it.

subtopic: PRELIMINARY STATEMENT OP ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
The preliminary statement of accounts was prepared in order to facilitate consideration, by a special committee of the house, of Canadian National matters as relating to the past year, and in the meantime every effort is being made by the management to get the completed accounts ready, together with the annual statement which accompanies them. Just as soon as that is in my hands I will be glad to table it in the house. I would call attention to the fact, however, that in former years 'any statement by the>
Minister of Railways has been made not in connection with the tabling of the accounts but in connection with the motion to refer the estimates to the special committee, and in fact there are several occasions upon which the minister might make such a statement as that mentioned by my hon. friend. In the meantime, we are merely enabling the committee to get along with its work. I am assured by the management that in previous

years there has been very little variation in the final audited statement of accounts from the preliminary statement which will be available for the members of the special committee, and I shall make ever effort to supply a complete statement of the accounts to all members of the house as soon as I possibly can.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
1.	Have legal proceedings been instituted against the Bronfman liquor interests (who operated in Saskatchewan) in accordance with the advice of the Hon. N. W. Rowell, K.C., counsel for the customs commission?
2.	What has been done regarding the evidence and exhibits submitted to the Department of Justice, on the advice of the Hon. N. W. Rowell, showing violations by the Bronfman company of, (a) the Criminal Code; (b) the Excise Act; (c) Food and Drug Act?
3.	AVhat has been done regarding the evasions by the above company of, (a) the income tax; (b) the business profits tax?

subtopic: E4ST END LIGHTHOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is practically imposible to make a categorical reply to the questions asked, and perhaps for that reason I might be permited to make a verbal explanation. The hon. member for Rosetown makes inquiry as to whether legal procedings have been taken against the Bronfman liquor interests in acordance with the advice of Hon. Mr. Rowell, who was the counsel for the royal commission investigating the Department of Customs. I might say that the recommendations come from the commission itself and not from Mr. Rowell.
The hon. member also asked for information regarding violations of the Criminal Code, the Excise Act and the Food and Drugs Act by what he calls the Bronfman company. I might say that as far as I know
Questions

there is no distinctive Bronfman company; as a matter of fact there are no fewer than twenty-eight companies and concerns in which the Bronfmans are interested, in addition to some twelve individuals. All these companies and individuals are now under investigation with regard to the possible collection of taxes which have not been paid. The records of these companies and individuals are more or less incomplete, and I think the house will understand when I say that to cover the records of so many concerns will require a considerable time, but these investigations are being pursued.
With regard to the matter of criminal prosecutions, there is only one recommendation in this connection from the commission itself. That recommendation is that action should be instituted against Harry Bronfman for the alleged bribery of a customs official in the city of Winnipeg. Some time ago counsel was employed through the Department of Justice to carry on this prosecution, but unfortunately considerable delay has been caused by reason of the prolonged illness of the chief witness, who is an officer of the customs department.
With regard to the violations of the Excise Act and the Food and Drugs Act, I may say there was no question of revenue involved in those violations, and as far as prosecutions are concerned, in the words of the commission itself conviction is now impossible by reason of the limitations in connection with such prosecutions.
I might just add in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that all the concerns as to which either investigations or prosecutions were recommended are being so investigated or prosecuted; I think I may say that without making any exceptions, and there are one hundred or more concerns mentioned in the report of the royal commission. They are all under investigation; in some cases prosecutions have actually taken place, and in a good many other instances we have collected the revenues concerned. I might add further that as far as the Department of National Revenue is concerned, we are taking action, and I assure the house that we will collect every dollar of revenue which is properly and legally owing to the government by the Bronfmans or by anyone else, for that matter.

speechtext:
1.	Are prisoners confined in penitentiaries throughout the Dominion permitted to receive and despatch letters from and to relatives and friends?
2.	If so, how many of such letters are they permitted to receive and send each month during their confinement ?
3.	Are there regulations prohibiting any correspondence until after the expiration of any specific time after their confinement?
4.	If so, what is said specific time?
5.	What provisions, if any, are made for prisoners' recreation or exercise?
6.	When a public holiday falls on a Monday are prisoners compelled to remain in their cells from the close of working time on Saturday until the following Tuesday morning?
7.	If not, for what purposes and under what conditions are they allowed out?
8.	Are the same regulations in force in all penitentiaries throughout Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRISONERS IN PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
1.	To or from relatives, yes; to or from friends, yes, if special circumstances require it.
2.	Inmates are permitted to receive all proper letters. Inmates are permitted to write one social letter to relatives each month; also all necessary letters to transact bona fide business; also should necessity arise, permission is granted to write " special letters."
3.	No. They may write as soon as received at the institution.
4.	See answer to No. 3.
5.	Inmates working on farm or at such outside employment are not given exercise. Instructions call for all other inmates employed in buildings, shops, etc. to have fifteen minutes outside exercise each forenoon and afternoon. A total of thirty minutes per day.
6.	Instructions issued are that should a holiday and Sunday come together inmates are to work one-half of the holiday. This does not apply, however, should Christmas fall on a Saturday or Monday, as on Christmas day they go to Church in the forenoon and are treated to concerts during the afternoon. On Sunday the inmates are out of their cells to their meals and also for the purpose of attending church.
7.	Answered by No. 6.
8.	Yes.
