The house resumed, from March 19, consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Heaps:
That, in the opinion of this house, the committee on industrial and international relations be authorized to investigate and report on insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity.
And the proposed amendment of Mr. Mc-Quarrie:
That the said resolution be amended by adding the following:
"That the said committee be authorized to investigate and report on the operations of companies carrying on sickness and accident insurance business in Canada."

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned on Monday evening, I was stating that in England and Denmark, they had tried to apply the system of supplementary pen-

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Deslauriers
sions, which perhaps would be the system approaching the nearest to the solution of the problem of invalidity, if it was backed by the good will of each individual and if the tendency to criticize did not impede its work, by making it difficult to consider requests for testing the system-prejudicing the minds of those making the inquiry to the extent of having them commit injustices. It is inadmissible that the state should directly force upon its citizens the art of making their savings thrive; it would be much more to the point to encourage, advise and guide them; however, we must submit to what is unavoidable and judge of the facts as they exist. All these systems, whether optional or not, are not adaptable when they are given a practical test. Some set the age for awards at 70, others at 60 or 65, but every day we see men capable of performing work-which they have for a long time done-with the greatest efficiency, and at a more advanced age than that fixed for pension. Must we declare them unfit and consider them entitled to annuities? Certainly not. Likewise, we sometimes come across a person under 60 years old, one who, although young, has become unfit through disease or he may simply be out of work and without hope of finding any; shall we oblige him to wait until he is 70 years old before coming to his assistance? Shall we content ourselves with blaming his lack of thrift? Which is not always the case, for very often ill luck has something to do with it. If therefore citizens have duties towards the state, on the other hand the state itself has duties towards its citizens, duties which it can fufill through special organizations, where individual thrift will be encouraged. All systems based on optional methods have had results that are not conclusive enough, for instance the subsidized optional insurance, voluntary assistance, charity, co-operation, economy reasonably practised, mutuality and participation in benefits; none of these systems have succeeded. That should lead us to advocate-while still having great regard for the freedom of individuals-thrift as enforced in Germany for a certain class of workers. This system has had good results-although not satisfactory enough, because a whole class, the great majority of which are included in the problem of invalidity and old age was set aside, leaving however to this moral person, the state, duties to fulfil towards 'lit. Moreover, if the state has the right to tax each individual, for the construction and upkeep of highways over which numerous citizens will never pass,
why should it not be in order to have a tax for the protection and support of the disabled?
Taking it as granted that it is impossible to find a perfect system owing to the imperfection and inequality of individuals, it is not the less true that we could find a remedy for many needs greatly simplifying the problem.
It is wrong to ascribe to lack of thrift alone the case of an indigent old person or of a disabled one. It may only be partly responsible, while uncontrollable circumstances in the life of individuals are mostly responsible for the problem. To guard against the lack of thrift and the ups and downs of life in all countries, thrift gave birth to insurance. By the same process, personal initiative has benefited many people, either by protecting them in the course of their activities, or by indemnifying them in cases of accidents, sickness, or again by allowing the person carrying an insurance policy, for life or for a limited period, credit of such nature as to inspire consideration and deference for his person on the part of hospitable people, benevolent and charitable societies; moreover of a nature to beget him the necessary cares of old age on the part of his own children. At that age especially, money seems to have great weight with people. But to benefit from an insurance, one condition is necessary: payments on the policy must be regularly made. This may be an easy matter when the person is young, full of health, earns steadily sufficient wages to keep up his policies; but what happens when, even during his period of activities, unemployment, accidents, misfortunes bear down upon him? It is possible that a certain number of individuals may have set aside sufficient savings to meet these contingencies, but the proportion is small among workers. What unfortunately happens with the great majority of them, is that they see their insurance policies cancelled, losing the necessary examination, admittance and regular disbursements, savings gathered through great sacrifices disappear in the vaults of insurance companies. They lose everything at an age when resources are most necessary. This is one of the factors of the problem of old age and invalidity.
The capital invested in all insurance associations or societies, to keep up an insurance policy, should be reimbursed to the insured on the discontinuation of payments on the policy, leaving to the companies the interest on such capital. That is only fair since the banks themselves follow that procedure and can afford to pay themselves dividends of 8 to 10 per cent and more.
1558	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Deslauriers
In most of the societies of mutual assistance, the proviso in their charter allowing the head office to increase the rates of payments according to the age of the insured, may be a necessary financial measure, but the facts are still there to show that in the period of youth and activity, people in health take out insurance policies easily kept up owing to their low rates of payment, and when unemployment-brought on by old age or sickness -stops the wages, it is then that the rates increase two-fold, three-fold and four-fold for those insured who have no other alternative than to mortgage their insurance policies to carry on their payments-and this means the cancelling of the policies within a few years, leaving the old people in poverty. These charters should be amended, otherwise legislators should refuse the granting of them thus closing the door through which comes part of the problem of invalidity.
If to-day, insurance protects people in various ways, which is admitted by everybody it is nevertheless the truth that at times it is the cause of poverty. This may seem a paradox but it is a fact. This altered relationship is so to apeak forced upon it by our legislation on labour in regard to employers' responsibilities -Of labour accidents.
The insurance companies grant to employers insurance policies for their employees, at rates based upon the age and the kind of risk which the work of the employee entails. Now, insurance companies know that generally, at the age of 45, the eyes of a man begin to show signs of myopy or hyperopia, that in certain work this affection may bring on a slight error in judgment and further render the employee liable to accidents, which may even prove fatal; they are aware that at this age, suppleness begins to disappear, a certain stiffness of the muscles and tendons is felt over the whole body, and involuntarily forces the worker, when he goes down the stairs, to strike each step many times with his heels, owing to a kind of nervous shaking which produces an unsteadiness of the legs; these companies know that the power of steadily gripping objects for the same reason begins to change and decrease, which added to impaired sight become a disadvantage for the employer and employee. It is then that insurance companies demand a high premium, even prohibitive; or they entirely refuse to insure the employee so as to protect the employer and themselves. The man working in the shop is then thanked for his services, at an age when he could still work more efficiently than a younger man not having his experience; once dismissed, it is difficult for

him to persuade people to employ him. That is the way a man who can work is declared unfit. The same may be said of a man working on high scaffolds, at 50 years old he is cast aside and no one will employ him, because the employer is not covered by insurance against accidents pertaining to work, and which are liable to happen to a man having reached a certain age. Consequently that workman dismissed as unfit, to whom work will be everywhere refused, first will miss his wages, then his few savings, if he has any, will dwindle down, he will therefore mortgage hie insurance policies and their cancellation will soon follow. Although enjoying relatively good health and capable1 of working, he will see himself classed among the unfit that poverty awaits. This is again a 'road upon which figures the contingent of old people in poverty and those who are forced to become unfit.
Our legislation on labour in relation to the employer's responsibilities towards the employee therefore gives rise precisely to the problem of premature old age and forced invalidity. Now, since we acknowledge such a state of affairs, should we not amend our labour legislation in regard to the employer's responsibilities in such a way, that insurance companies should have no power to cancel policies, and the employer should not be held responsible towards the employee, who has reached a certain age limit and would like to carry on his work?
No doubt we cannot force upon an insurance company rules for its risk rates-that is its business-no more than we can oblige an employer to hire such and such a worker. Labour legislation must be so amended as to allow the workman at any age to earn his living by utilizing his energies such as they are. The state should found a social insurance in which might be admitted any person having reached the age of 40, with special rates or even make up the deficiency existing in various rates. This insurance would be taken care by a tax on successions, by unclaimed balances in banks, by industries which have profited by his toils and by a contribution of the insured. In this way the contingent of disabled and indigent old people would be much decreased. If we include in our legislation what seems to have given the best results in other countries, that is supplementary pension for the unfit whatever be his age or the cause of invalidity, it is most likely that this problem, for so long the object of investigations, would be solved within the limits which are possible to humaD beings.

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Edwards
There are duties that devolve upon those who have wealth, towards society and the poor. In any stock-taking the manufacturer must make certain allowance for depreciation of his plant, machinery, tools and goods; why should he not make a certain allowance for depreciation of his human stock: his workmen, his clerks? The rich man must not only play in society the part of receiver withholding all he receives, but also that of a charitable channel spreading around him favours under the guise of insurance against unemployment or old age. If it is necessary the state should allow for such acts by remitting to him certain custom and excise dues or other taxes.
I shall quote on the subject the views of a celebrated economist: "Charity, moreover, is, for the person who practises it, a source of joy, wealth-like the intellect, speech, activity-was bestowed on man not for himself but for others as water was given to the mountain not to remain there but to flow and fertilize the plain. Look at this water leaping from rock to rock, cascade to cascade, on the hillside it is joyous, it sings and casts on its shores the pearls of its foam and song. Why? Because it obeys its law and fulfils its mission of bringing joy and fecundity to the countryside. It is the image of the soul that gives, devotes itself and lives for others. On the contrary look at the stagnant and greenish water in the* hollow of the rock: it is dull and gloomy, putriscent and nauseous; it puts to flight the birds of heaven. Why? Because it should be a living water and it is dead. It is the image of the selfish soul folding within itself and finding in its own selfishness but a mortal weariness. We must live for others, and be the beautiful river which carries its wealth to towns and countryside, we must be generous according to our means, like the humble stream meandering through the meadows. We must be the drop of water which added to other drops is carried away to swell the river. Pray! let us not be marshes."

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with
considerable interest to the discussion which has taken place on the motion moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and the amendment moved 'by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie). Nothing more tragic 'has ever been portrayed on the stage of a theatre than the scenes we meet with every day in the general walks of life throughout the country. No more tragic picture, it seems to me, can be presented for
the consideration of anyone who would like to solve these problems than that of a man who has done his best in life, who 'has played the game fairly with whatever intelligence he has and with the best of objects in view, and Who yet has proved, through unfortunate circumstances, a failure or what, generally speaking, would be called a failure. The unfortunate circumstances might have been in the shape of a period of ill health which he could not control; or he might have been kid off or unable to get work when he was anxious to work. There is often a tendency to regard that man, who is in poor circumstances, struggling hard to get along and to make a fair living for his wife and children, as a failure. That is unfair to any man who has utilized his best efforts and shown a willingness to work when work was available. That man deserves some consideration at the hands of the government of the country in which he lives.
I was very much impressed with statements made in the course of his remarks by the hon. member for Comox-A'lberni (Mr. Neill). He painted a picture which I regard as a true one; it is not overdrawn, so far as I can see, in any particular, and I have read his speech very carefully. He refers to the situation of a man who is on half time or part time or who has no work at all, who finds expenses crowding upon him and who is obliged to cut down the living of his family in order to meet his meagre purse, and to the economic effect of that man's situation on the country at large. The man is unemployed through no fault of his own; his being out of work lessens his power to buy, and this tends to create unemployment in manufacturing industries. That is an argument which struck me as reasonable and sound in every particular. The very fact that the man is out of employment himself and his purchasing power has been thereby decreased makes him a very important factor in producing further unemployment in the country.
Another point which was raised by the hon. member in regard to wages caught my eye. He made the following statement:
If he cannot get W'ork at his own particular trade he will break into some other branch of work, which generally means the casual labour market, thereby aggravating the condition because there is no more work in that market than before. Consequently he has to steal or share some other man's work, which generally means lower wages for both of them, and iurther decreases their purchasing power.
That brought to my mind a thought which I want to speak on for just a few moments, and that is the question of wages. If I might venture to refer to the country across the
1560	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Edwards
line without irritating some hon. gentlemen to the right of the Speaker, I think I am correct in saying that in the United States of America they claim that they are paying the highest scale of wages of any country in the world. They also claim that as regards their labouring or wage-earning classes, they have the highest standard of living of any people similarly engaged in any country in the world. I believe it is largely if not entirely true that, covering the United States of America, the scale of wages is perhaps higher than in any other country, and largely because of that liberal or high scale of wages the standard of living of the wage-earning classes in the United States is possibly as high if not higher than that of wage-earners in any other country in the world.
As this resolution deals with the question of insurance against unemployment, is it not wise to look this matter in the face and ask ourselves what has brought about this state of affairs in the United States? If the proposition is correct that the standard of living and scale of wages in the United States are high as compared with other countries, then it does seem to me that it is reasonable and logical to assume that that condition in the United States, to which their statesmen refer so frequently and so loudly, in praise of themselves, is largely if not entirely attributable to the fiscal policy adapted in that country. Take any class of people that you like in the United States, and what do you find? Even before the war the United States of America was a country with a very high protective tariff wall, but immediately following the war the United States took this position. They said: "We have within the bounds of our country a population of considerably over one hundred millions, and we do not propose to permit the people of other countries, with their cheap labour, to enter our market when the United States is excluded from their markets largely because of the cheap labour which prevails in these European countries which were engaged in the war, and also because of the fact that those countries which were devastated by the war are not in a position to buy our products. We therefore will protect our producers of every class in the United States against the low wage scale of the countries of Europe which were engaged in the war and devastated by the war, and also from the effects of their depreciated and disturbed currency. We will protect our producers in the United States against that unfair competition." I submit that that was a reasonable and sound position for the United States to take, and they have followed that policy wherever any

one of their industries or any class of their people have been exposed to what they consider the unfair competition of the products of Canada or any other country. They have at once, through the power given to their president, put on an embargo or taken other means to keep out of their country the articles which were coming into competition with the products of their own industry. The result has been that in the United States their factories have been running, protected as they are against what they regard as the unfair competition and the low wage scale of Great Britain and the countries of continental Europe, and their people have been employed because their factories have been running. There has also been encouragement for production on the farms in the United States through the tariffs which they have imposed against Canada and other countries in order to protect their own farm products from the cheap production of the Argentine and other countries with a lower wage scale and a lower cost of production. I mention those facts, and I invite to them the attention especially of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house, particularly the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), who, because of the position he occupies, must shed some tears over the unemployment that exists in this country, whether he feels like it or not; he would not be playing the game with labour if he did not show that he was a little concerned about the unemployment question; and I would appeal also to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), to the philosopher from South Huron (Mr. McMillan), and others on the other side of the house, to my good friend from Saskatoon (Mr. Young), for instance, whom I see and who might give consideration to this matter-

I rise to a
point of order, Mr. Speaker. The resolution before the house is very definite and specific, and I submit that what the hon. gentleman is discussing has nothing whatever to do with the resolution. The question before us is the further consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Heaps:
That, in the opinion of this house, the committee on industrial and international relations be authorized to investigate and report on insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity, and of the amendment thereto of Mr. McQuarrie.
Now, what the hon. member is attempting to discuss is the possible causes leading up to unemployment, and that has nothing whatever to do with the motion on the order paper. I would suggest that this house would get

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Edwards
along more quickly and do its business better if hon. members were kept more closely to the question immediately before us.
I do not consider the hon. gentleman's remarks irrelevant at all. He is leading up to the question before the house.

The hon. member for
Saskatoon just wanted to make a little speech.

I am very
glad indeed to have the interjection of my genial friend from Saskatoon. I think perhaps now he will be relieved of any obligation to make a speech when his turn comes, because he will have already shown by what he has said and put on the pages of Hansard his very deep interest in this matter. I may say, however, in regard to the point which he raised, and it is a very blunt point, that I felt justified in speaking as I did. Mr. Speaker, because I note that at page 1562 of Hansard the hon. gentleman who introduced this motion said:
I do not agree with that particular viewpoint. I believe unemployment is a problem that ought to be faced by the Dominion government. In this house we deal with and pass legislation that has a direct bearing upon this all-important question. We deal with facts, immigration matters, trade treaties, foreign policies, banking laws, and all these I claim affect the volume of employment or unemployment in this country.
I am sure the hon. member for Saskatoon would not be so hard hearted as not to give me the same consideration that he gave to the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), and I do not find recorded on Hansard that he raised any objection to the hon. member for North Winnipeg introducing the tariff and trade matters as having a bearing on the question before us; and the mover of the resolution having brought up that point, I therefore felt I was perfectly justified, Mr. Speaker, in enlarging upon it. The point that I was endeavouring to impress upon the hon. member for Saskatoon, the hon. member for South Huron, and one or two other hon. gentlemen, including the Minister of Labour, was that in the United States they do to a large extent solve this very problem, of unemployment by adopting a fiscal policy which gives employment to their own people. The hon. member for Saskatoon knew perfectly well what I was coming at, but I want to state it in so many words so that there will be no doubt about it. The point I was coming to was this:	In this resolution we are dealing
with a very important question, the question of unemployment in Canada, and if the hon. member for Saskatoon and the genial philosopher from South Huron will add their
eloquence and logic to that of the Minister of Labour, with perhaps a few words of advice thrown in by the Minister of Agriculture, and one or two others, they will perhaps be able to impress on the minds of the government the important bearing which the mistaken fiscal policy they have followed has upon unemployment in this country. As an illustration, if we were to give the encouragement Which should be given too the production of wool in this country to meet our own requirements, it would afford employment to over seventy thousand people. Surely that has a direct relation to this question of unemployment. But the mistaken policy followed by this government and supported by these hon. gentlemen, including even the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), has practically put our sheep industry out of business. Yet that is an industry which ought to be encouraged, and which, if encouraged, would solve unemployment to the extent of providing occupation for tens of thousands of Canadians. I submit it is reasonable to point that out to the house.
I might call attention to one or two other things. I sincerely wish I could impress the importance of this upon the government. Take, for instance, our dairy industry. There is absolutely no question that tens of thousands of our farmers could be given a chance to establish themselves in the dairy industry if it were not for the mistaken fiscal policy of this government in allowing the importation of tens of millions of pounds of butter from Australia and New Zealand. These importations have absolutely discouraged tens of thousands of Canadians from establishing dairy herds. That has a very direct application to the resolution proposed by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), because if you are to authorize the committee on Industrial and International Relations to investigate and report on insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity, that committee is bound to consider as many causes of unemployment as they can find; in a word, the committee must investigate all the factors which enter into unemployment. I am presenting some of those factors which I think the committee should investigate and report upon.
It is just as important for that committee to point out to the people of this country how unemployment can be prevented as it is to devise ways and means of dealing with unemployment after we have it. The old saying applies in this case as in others, "A stitch in time saves nine," and I do submit in all seriousness that it is our duty to con-

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Robb
sider whether or not the fiscal policy pursued by the government has a tendency to create unemployment. If it does have that tendency, then manifestly it is incumbent upon us to get rid of the cause, for by so doing we will be helping to reduce unemployment in the Dominion. I present that argument to the house in all seriousness and in the belief that it is sound. I was induced to present it after reading the speech of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni in regard to lower wages and their meaning. I know there is a mistaken notion abroad in the minds of some political economists that a tariff always increases the price of the article to the consumer. I do not agree with that for a moment. The position is untenable. If you take some article which is not produced in Canada, for instance, tea, and put a tax on it, then perhaps you will make the people pay the full amount of the tax; but if a tax is imposed upon an article which is also produced in this country, then I say he who claims that that tax increases the cost not only of the article imported but also of the article of a similar kind made in Canada, is taking a position that is absolutely untenable. I mention that because again it comes back to the question of a correct fiscal policy for the dominion and its relation to unemployment.
I notice the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is doing me the honour of paying attention to my remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear. I am admiring you.

I feel very
much flattered by the hon. minister's admiration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I offer it modestly.

I am indeed pleased. I hope he will take advantage of his great influence in this house and his legal training to do me the further honour of pointing out, if he can, wherein my argument is lame or weak, that the mistaken fiscal policy of the government, has a direct bearing upon unemployment. I repeat, the whole matter of emigration is intimately related to unemployment. Tens of thousands of our boys and girls have emigrated to the United States. Why? Because they could not get employment' at home. I say it is up to this or any other government seriously to consider to what extent the fiscal policy which has been followed is responsible for this exodus. What is the use of devising remedies and applying medicine after the patient is dead? The fact is that since the government came into power

we have lost, some six hundred thousand Canadians to the United States because of lack of employment in this country'. They could not get employment at home because the fiscal policy of the government has given no encouragement to industry or to agriculture, and consequently there have been no opportunities for employment of our people.
I think it is more logical and reasonable all round to give consideration to how best we can prevent unemployment rather than to spend time and effort in an attempt to devise some form of insurance to meet the situation, which, in my opinion, might be very largely met by a decided' change in our fiscal policy.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time that I have had occasion to address the house under the forty-minute rule but I wish to assure you that I shall not occupy my full time. I rise to say on behalf of the government that we are favourable to the passage of this resolution so that it may go to a committee to investigate in all its bearings the question of insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity.
But, sir, I have to point out that the amendment offered by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) is not at all in line with this resolution. It introduces practically a different question which should go to another committee, that on banking and commerce, and I would ask my hon. friend or someone on his behalf to withdraw the amendment so that we may vote in favour of the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No doubt there is some dissatisfaction on the part of the public regarding the cancellation of accident and sickness insurance policies, but there is this to be said for such policies, that they are only yearly, subject to renewal at the option of the insurer. The alternative would be to establish a system of non-cancellable policies. This form of policy has already been tried and the experience of the companies has been that it is not profitable. Many spurious claims, it is intimated, have been put in from time to time so that the companies do not find it profitable to issue non-cancellable accident and sickness insurance. If all the claims were as fair and just as that of my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) I fancy there would be little difficulty in establishing that system of insurance; but apparently the claims have not been of that character. If that form of insurance has been found unprofitable by the companies, I ask hon. gentlemen representing various parties in the house

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. McQuarrie
whether in their opinion it would prove more profitable if administered by the government. I leave that thought with the house. I would suggest that as my hon. friend's amendment relates more particularly to .accident and sickness insurance, he might very well withdraw it and if he desired to make further enquiry into the complaints disclosed in his observations of the other day he might move another resolution to refer the matter to the banking and commerce committee.

I did not suggest that the companies should be required to issue any policy which they would be compelled to renew; I made that perfectly plain. My point was that insurance companies carrying on this class of business should not be allowed to cancel policies while the insured was in such a condition, owing to the illness which he sustained during the existence of the original policy, that he could not get insurance from other companies. I will agree with everything the minister has said regarding the impossibility of requiring companies to issue policies which are renewable until the expiration of the time limit, that is to say, the number of years one is insurable. But in the case I refer to-and this is happening every day- where a man becomes ill the companies do one of two things, if his illness is serious: they eliminate the illness or refuse to renew the policy. In my own particular case I found myself in a position where my policy was practically cancelled; the company refused to renew it. On the date it expired I received notice to that effect. Then I found that other companies, for a certain period at least, would not take me at all because of the refusal of the first company to renew the original policy. This, it seems to me, is a risk which these insurance companies might fairly be expected to take. That is my point. I did not suggest at all that the companies be required to issue policies renewable for all time. I have no intention in the world of interfering in any way with the resolution moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), and if my amendment is going to have the effect of killing his resolution I will not press it at the moment. There is this difficulty, however, that it may be impossible for me to move and have discussed during the present session a resolution with reference to the point I am now submitting to the house. I suppose I could allow the matter to stand until another session, but it seems to me that the operations of these insurance companies should be controlled in some way. If they are conducting their business in an arbitrary and 36103-100
unfair manner there should be some means of regulating them. Certainly the present condition is nothing short of a scandal, and there are hon. members in this house, a number of them, whose experience has been similar to mine. Surely when you take out health insurance you should get something for your money. I am afraid that these companies are prepared to take people's money so long as the insured remain well, but when they become -a risk the companies simply slide out, refusing to renew the policy. I suppose they are privileged to do this under the law as it stands; but the law should be changed. That was what I had in mind when moving the amendment; I did not intend to force any company to give me a sickness policy- I trust I can get along without one. I sincerely hope that this whole matter will be investigated by some committee, and I thought that inasmuch as my hon. friend's resolution referred to sickness insurance it would be proper at the same time to investigate the operations of companies carrying on that class of business to-day. I cannot see any objection to this proposal, but I wish to make it perfectly clear that I do not insist upon my amendment if its effect is to destroy the original motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand my hon. friend is prepared to withdraw his amendment. I shall be glad to facilitate, so far as I can, the submission of his complaint to the banking and commerce committee. With much of what he has said I agree.
Amendment withdrawn.
Motion agreed to.

Whereas the market for the output of British Columbia coal mines is seriously reduced by the competition of fuel oil imported at an enormous cost;
And whereas scientific research in Britain and elsewhere has demonstrated that coal, when used in a highly pulverized form, can successfully compete in price and results, with fuel oil;
And whereas it is very desirable that the output of our mines should be increased and more labour employed;
Therefore be it resolved-that, in the opinion of this house, in order to test and demonstrate the possibilities of pulverized coal, the government should adapt one of their steamers on the Pacific coast, and the furnace of one of the government public buildings in British Columbia, to the use of pulverized coal from Vancouver island mines.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is another of the many coal resolutions we have had this session, but it is unique in two respects: in the first

Pulverized Coal-Mr. Neill

place I do not call it a national coal policy, and in the second place I do not ask other portions of Canada to be saddled with enormous burdens of taxation in order to assist the particular part of the country in which I am interested. In this resolution I merely ask the government by a small expenditure to put us in a position whereby we can help ourselves, which is the very best form of assistance anyone can ask or receive from any government.
In British Columbia during recent years we have been suffering from the competition of fuel oil imported from the United States. Ten or fifteen years ago the exports of coal from the Vancouver island mines to San Francisco were so large that the operators maintained offices there for the disposal of the coal, but that condition has long since passed away. We do not ship any coal to San Francisco now, but we import enormous quantities of fuel oil. During the first half of 1927 we imported 59,000,000 gallons of oil on which duty was paid, in addition to which large quantities were brought in by the steamship companies in bond, which were used by them without that importation being recorded in the customs returns. Making an approximate allowance for the amount so brought in, and taking that into consideration we find that in British Columbia alone we pay something like S5,000,000 a year to the United States for fuel oil. That is equivalent to about 600,000 tons of coal, or nearly one-half the annual output of the Vancouver island coal mines to-day. The production of that quantity of coal would support a town with a population of some 5,000 or 6,000, and since we neither eat nor wear coal this would mean an increased demand for the products of the soil and for the manufactured goods of the east, therefore this is not a purely local question.
From time to time we have naturally looked about us for something which will offset this importation of fuel oil, and the first thing that was suggested by our Conservative friends was a tariff on that article. On one occasion an election was held mainly on that issue. I well recall that about the year 1922 I went to Hon. Mr. Fielding, the then Minister of Finance, asking him to increase the duty on fuel oil; as I went into his office I saw a large number of gentlemen, and indeed I might say a large number of large gentlemen, coming out. They were of the class described by Shakespeare as fat men, bulky, thick, well-fed, sleekdooking gentlemen, evincing every aspect of prosperity, and as they came out I eyed them with some curiosity. Then I went in to see the minister, and humbly proffered my claim for an increased duty on fuel oil. With IMr. Neill.]
that simplicity which characterized me in those days, and indeed does so yet, I said, "Why, Mr. Fielding, the Conservatives will support you in increasing the duty because they pledged themselves to do so in the recent election, and moreover it is a part of their fiscal policy." The kindly old gentleman smiled at me with his eyes tired with half a century's experience of politics and said, "Mr. Neill, did you see those gentlemen who went out just as you oame in?" I said, "Yes, what about them?" He said, "They were a deputation from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association asking that the duty be removed altogether."
I wondered to myself what hope I, a poor, lean, hungry Cassius, could have to compete with those numerous fat, sleek-looking Fal-staffs whom I had seen, but with the courage of despair I said to Mr. Fielding, "If we cannot have protection, then let us have free trade in coal," because that would benefit us to the same extent. Owing to the way the tariff is arranged, on the basis of reciprocity with the United States, free trade would mean that if we reduced our tariff in the east our coal from the west would enter the markets of the United States to a much larger extent. But Mr. Fielding pointed out to me very truly and very correctly that there were sixteen members from Nova Scotia all asking for a higher duty on coal, and he also made clear how disastrous the effect would be on the Nova Scotia coal miners if the duty were to be removed altogether. It was then brought home to me how difficult it is to reconcile the different sections of Canada to any one form of fiscal policy, so it was apparent that we had little to hope for from any tinkering with the tariff in that regard.
The next thing that suggested itself was the possibility of the further manufacture of this coal;, that is, that we should not sell the coal in its raw state but should manufacture it into what might be called its ultimate products, such as gasoline, benzine and other coal tar products. I was much attracted by reports appearing in the press which stated that in Germany, by means of what is known as the Bergius process, they had actually obtained gasoline from coal in quantities which were said to be commercially remunerative. I looked into that matter, but with very little success. I have in my hand an extract from the debates of the English House of Commons containing a question asked when I was there last year; a member of the house asked the government what the prospects were of applying in England a process which he called the low-temperture carbonization process, and which he claimed had been successful in Ger-

Pulverized Coal-Mr. Neill
many. He asked why that process could not be applied in Great Britain, and the member of the government who replied stated that he was not aware of any low temperature process being used successfully on a commercial scale, in connection with the type of coal available in England. So we found that while that process was adaptable in Germany, either because of t'he class of coal or the cheapness with which it could be produced, it could not be applied profitably to the coal mines of Britain. There was a meeting of the mining and metallurgical association in British Columbia last summer, and those attending that meeting stated that their technical and scientific information was to the effect that with t'heir present knowledge it w'ould be at least many years before it would be commercially possible to extract gasoline from the type of coal we have on Vancouver island. It is also impossible to convert that coal into gas, because the distance to the centres of consumption would be too great to transport the gas in pipes.
Well, Mr. Speaker, when we failed in that regard we continued looking around for a remedy, and it was suggested by this meeting of scientific experts last summer that the solution of the problem was the use of pulverized coal. The use of pulverized coal is not a fad. In the United States something like 50.000,000 tons a year are used in various plants throughout the country. In the state of Washington, adjoining British Columbia, alone, there are seven plants which use 320,000 tons of coal a year in that way. In the United states the navy has been interested in this subject, and they have been carrying on experiments for years. On one occasion quite recently they made a test of a Scotch marine boiler; it was the common type, the best type of boiler used on ships, and they ran it on pulverized coal for 240 hours continuously with very satisfactory results. It produces no smoke and no dust, and you can see the possibilities or advantages from the use of a fuel of that kind in the cities. So much so that the United States authorities made arrangements to equip a steamship called the Mercer, I think it was, on a trip from some port in the United States to Rotterdam ; and it is on record that when that boat reached Rotterdam there were representatives of England, Germany, France, Italy, Norway, Sweden and Holland present, representing shipping companies, public utility companies, and government navies, all on the qui vive and highly interested to se/' the results of the trip, what the effect had been on the boilers, and so forth. The result of the Tound trip was that they saved three days' 56103-lOOi
time and something like 30 per cent of the cost of the fuel as compared with the cost of the fuel oil with which the same boat had been previously equipped. The United States navy afterwards issued a statement to the effect that the test had been one of the most severe that it was possible to carry out, and they were thoroughly satisfied with the use of pulverized coal on steamships at the present time.
If that is so satisfactory, if that is ascertained, so to speak, it may be asked: why the purpose of this resolution which asks the government to more or less experiment by means of equipping a boat, and one of their public building furnaces, with machinery to use pulverized coal? Well, the answer is this: Each of these factories where coal has been used presents an entirely separate new problem. There are many things about the conditions that we do not know yet. Every individual class of coal has to be tested. The amount of ash, the amount of sulphur, and the moisture that it contains are all factors that go to determine whether that particular coal can be pulverized, and what kind of equipment is necessary to handle it. For instance something hinges on what is called the length of the flame. If a flame of a certain length can be produced that is of great advantage. And then, of course, there is the further question of the particular type of boiler adapted to that particular coal. All these questions need to be decided by actual experiment. And then there is another thing. We know that money is very conservative- and money means business, and business means money. Capitalists are not prone to take up new ideas unless they are sure of the advantages that will result from them. We all know how the internal combustion engine-what is known as the motor car to-day-hung fire for many years. It was well known for many years before it was introduced in a commercial way. The same thing can be said of the telephone and various other inventions. They lay dormant for a long time.
Now much has been said of recent years in connection with research, particularly this session and last session, and I think the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and myself are entitled to some little credit, because I can recall that we advocated research years ago and we got very little sympathy and very little attention on the matter. W ell, this is a typical instance of very moderately expensive research. To demonstrate its advantages would involve very small expense, and it would be of great benefit even to the government, because if they equipped their boats on the Pacific ocean it would be a

Pulverized. Coal-Mr. Kaiser
great saving to them. Even on the hydrographic boats the use of smokeless fuel would be of great advantage. It would give an impetus to our coal mines and react on other lines of business not only in British Columbia, but throughout the Dominion.
I therefore trust that the government will see their way to give this fuel a fair trial by equipping one of their steamers with the machinery necessary to use pulverized coal, and also permit one of their public buildings, either in the city of Vancouver or the city of Victoria, to use pulverized coal from the mines of Vancouver island.

There may be some confusion in the minds of certain people in regard to this resolution, as compared with the one that I introduced in the house at an earlier date. I wish to say that these two propositions do not conflict in any way whatever. I am inclined very much to support this particular resolution, and I think the government would do well to give it their attention.
Just by way of showing the particular difference there is between this suggestion and the one that I submitted, and the attitude assumed by different people in regard to it, I should like to read to the house' a letter which I have just received from the University of Birmingham, England, in regard to the proposition that has been discussed in this house. I am decidedly in favour of any move in regard to research or experimental work in connection with coal. I believe it to be among the great questions, in fact one of the most important, that will bring wonderful results to our country and to the people of the British Empire if the course which we advocate is followed.
The following letter was addressed to me by Mr. J. Ivon Graham, Experimentalist of the University mentioned. He writes as follows:
Dear Sir:
I have been much interested in your letter of the 14th February, regarding your lignite coal and the possibility of converting this into oil by the Bergius hydrogenation process. We shall be very pleased to carry out some tests upon representative samples of the lignite. You will understand, of course, that our work is being carried out on a purely laboratory scale, the amount of sample being dealt with in our high pressure bomb being only about i pound. Nevertheless, we consider that these tests give a good indication of the results which may be expected by the treatment of the coal on a much larger scale.
We should be very pleased to have one or two of your university graduates in chemistry for the purpose of studying the process here, though I am afraid our limited laboratory accommodation would not permit at the moment

more than two additional investigators. I think, however, it would be advisable if, in the first place, preliminary tests were carried out by us to ascertain whether the process appeared to have financial possibilities. We shall be only too glad to carry out these tests without making any charge as the treatment of various types of fuel by the hydrogenation process is of considerable interest to us from the research point of view. Should you be able to arrange for samples of your coal to be forwarded to us we shall be glad to have at least 5 pounds of each.
I have pleasure in enclosing herewith a reprint of a recent paper which summarises the work carried out in this laboratory.
Yours faithfully,
J. Ivon Graham.
I merely read this letter to show how sympathetic the laboratory people are in regard to our request. I think this letter will give some useful information to the Minister of the Interior and the government.
In conclusion I simply desire to say that I think we should support the resolution and should move in a direction that will tend towards the processing and the utilization of our coal deposits in a manner other than those which are being used at the present time.

I am
in full accord with the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). I am anxious to do anything I can to assist the coal mining industry of Vancouver island. I was fortunate in being a guest at the meeting in the city of Nanaimo of the scientific gentlemen as mentioned by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and they discussed at length the question of the liquefaction of coal. We had present a very distinguished gentleman from the United States, a thorough scientist. The consensus of opinion at that meeting was that the liquefaction of coal was still too far in the future to prove of any benefit to the mines of Vancouver island or of Canada generally. The liquefaction of coal has been accomplished as a laboratory experiment, it has even gone beyond that point, but the cost is so great that there would be no advantage in attempting to liquefy the coal of Vancouver island.
There would seem to be some possibilities with respect to the pulverization of coal, but in a conversation I had with the manager of one of the principal mining enterprises on the island-the hon. member for Comox-Alberni doubtless knows him quite well- he seemed to think there were serious difficulties in the way of pulverizing coal and using it on steamers. It is quite well understood that the coal would have to be pul-

Pulverized, Coal-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
verized just as it would be used, because, as it is gaseous, it would be dangerous to put coal dust on board a steamer or even on board a locomotive. Therefore the suggestion was that it would be pulverized just as it would be used. Coal differs greatly in quality, and in length of the flame and these facts taken in conjunction with the liability of the nozzles to plug up had militated against the general use of pulverized coal but he hoped these difficulties might be overcome. That gentleman, however, was not enthusiastic over it, neither were any of the other gentlemen at the meeting at which I was present. I can see no reason why the difficulties cannot be overcome and pulverized coal be used on our locomotives and our steamboats leaving the Pacific coast. If that pulverized coal can be used, it will be of great benefit to an industry that has been struggling for existence in that part of thei country for years. Some of our mines have Ibeen closed down for years and others are working only on part time. Owing to difficult structural conditions with respect to the geology of our mining field, it costs a little more to produce that coal than it costs to produce coal in other fields. When it is produced, it is a better quality of coal and the question is just one of dollars and cents whether we can do something that will give relief to the industry. Therefore I have great pleasure in supporting in the strongest manner possible the resolution moved by; the hon. member for Comox-Albemi.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government
have no objection for two reasons, to the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). The principal one is that- this is no longer an experiment, nor is it in the laboratory stage. The second reason is that the greatest competitor of coal at the moment on the west coast, indeed in connection with shipping generally, is fuel oil. That is true not only in Canada but in Great Britain and on the continent as well. Nearly every passenger ship plying on the Atlantic and the Pacific to-day is fueled with oil, with the result that the coal industries of Canada, Britain and elsewhere are all feeling the serious effects of this competition. Their hope was that perhaps the supply of fuel oil would not be of long duration, but it looks, by the fresh discoveries that are being made from day to day, as though this situation will continue for a number of years to come. Not only is that the case, but there is the fact of the introduction of gas
into general use in Canada, and the introduction of natural gas in my own province, because notwithstanding the fact that the city of Edmonton is located on top of a coal field and Calgary is adjacent to one, I suppose by far the largest percentage of domestic heating is done there to-day with natural gas. So in all directions the market for coal is being infringed upon by substitutes that are being used generally. In this very city a large percentage of the domestic heating to-day is being done by the use of fuel oil. Then there was the introduction of hydro-electric energy and it is estimated that in Canada alone the use of hydro-electric energy as a substitute for coal for power purposes has made a diminution in the coal market all told of almost. 27,000,000 tons. This means a tremendous displacement in the fuel market adversely affecting the coal industry.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni has covered the ground pretty well, as did the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Kaiser) to-day in connection with the hydrogenation of coal for the production of oil. This afternoon the discussion centres around the use of pulverized coal. Last summer when I was in England I was greatly interested in what they had been doing there, and I was assured by marine engineers that on vessels that were then being laid down, particularly the freighters, it was the intention of the engineers who had designed those vessels, to substitute pulverized coal for fuel oil. They stated that on present-day prices there would be a saving by this substitution of almost twenty per cent in fuel costs. Therefore there seems to be rather a bright future for pulverized fuel if it can be succesfully used as they think it can, particularly upon our freighters, and it will bring back a market that is now being denied the coal industry, as I said before, not only in Canada, but in Great Britain and on the continent. The government accordingly rather welcome the suggestion of the hon. member that an experiment be made upon one of their merchant marine vessels as well as an experiment in one of the large public buildings in the city of Vancouver, in order to test out the possibilities of using pulverized coal from the mines of British Columbia. What my hon. friend has said is very true, namely, that not all the products of the mines in any given locality can be successfully pulverized and a test is by no means conclusive when it is done upon a laboratory scale; but when pulverized coal is tried out in this way on a commercial scale, the test will be conclusive as to the utility of the coal from any given mine for use either on board ship or for

National Service

Mr. Irvine
heating purposes in the furnaces commonly found in our large buildings or our homes. I have spoken both to the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and I have their consent to have this test made as speedily as arrangements can be made in that regard.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSCRIPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND ESSENTIAL SERVICES IN TIME OF WAR
PROPOSED CONSCRIPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND ESSENTIAL SERVICES IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext:
Whereas, it is the existent policy of this country, that reasonable preparation should be made for self-defence in case of any war involving Canada;
And whereas, such preparation if undertaken, should be both adequate, and of such a character as to make war less likely to occur;
Therefore be it resolved-that, in the opinion of this house, it is advisable that legislation be enacted providing that on the declaration of war involving Canada, all natural resources and essential services, including transportation facilities, industrial plants and commercial and financial agencies, should automatically be conscripted for national service for the duration of the war.
He said: Mr. Speaker, whatever hon. members may think of the merits of the proposal contained in this resolution, or whatever they may think of the practicability of giving effedt to it in legislation, I hope they will regard my motives as sincere and] grant me the generous thought that my sole purpose in introducing the resolution is for the future protection and happiness of our country.
Since Your Honour has been invested with the authority to enforce observance of the rules of the house, and in doing so must chop me off precisely forty minutes from the moment I commence to address you, I shall first take the precaution to indicate the main grounds upon which I shall urge the. adoption of this resolution by parliament, and then if my hour should strike before I have finished, I shall be consoled somewhat with the thought that I have at least mentioned the steps in the argument which lead towards the desired conclusion.
I shall argue that since world conditions are such as to warrant the annual expenditures for war preparations which we now make, we would be illogical and unsafe guardians of the state if we did not recognize the principle that since there is cause for any preparation whatsoever, we are without excuse if we do not make the fullest preparation possible.
I shall then advance the idea that the acceptance of the proposal as set forth in this

resolution, namely, that it is advisable that legislation be enacted providing that on the declaration of war involving Canada all natural resources and essential services, including transportation facilities, industrial plants and commercial and financial agencies, should automatically be conscripted for national service for the duration of the war, would ensure adequate preparation for national defence at no additional cost to the state.
Next, I shall! endeavour to establish the view that the profit incentive in time of war is a real menace to peace, and if removed by the conscription measure suggested in the resolution, then one of the causes of war would be removed, and to that extent we should have a greater assurance of lasting peace.
Finally, I shall show that a war could be fought under the conditions proposed without leaving 'behind it a national debt to burden posterity.
The present policy of this government, as of preceding governments in this country, is one of preparation for defence. That preparation, I presume, is justified by certain fears which we legitimately hold, feare Which arise out of unsettled international conditions. Now, if there are good' grounds for the preparations which we now make, there must be equally good grounds for the most efficient preparation possible. I want to point out in this connection that a well trained, well disciplined, and well generated force of fighting men is not the only factor in national defence. Indeed, I would go further and say thait it is peifhaps the least important factor. I know of no modern war which has been lost for lack of soldiers. Service and heroism in the battle line have always been more in evidence than service and heroism in industry, in finance or in commerce, and yet surely to a country that is fighting for its existence these are of equal importance with the army in the front line. A country I think can nearly always rely upon its citizens responding to a call to arms in its defence, but it cannot always rely upon the other agencies which are equally necessary in times of naitiional danger. Past wars have been the soldier's opportunity to die, industry's opportunity to make money, and the country's opportunity to assume eternal debt. Conditions in these respects have grown to such a pitch in modem wars that unless some such proposal as I have made be adopted, a nation in the future will lose even more by winning a war than by being defeated, for when the price of victory has already been

National Service-Mr. Irvine
paid by the nation in blood, posterity will have to pay the profiteers for all time in a monetary form for t'he victory which the country has achieved.
How is it that national defence in Canada to-day, as in most other countries, I presume, is confined to the training of that element which requires the least training? A man with a rifle in one hand and his life in the other is thought to need a great deal of training, and so we spend a good deal of money in training him, but a man with the national credit in one hand and the right to charge interest in the other requires no training at all, according to our military program. But, as I have already said, these agencies, financial, industrial and commercial, do not know what to do in time of war for the national defence or in the national interest. These agencies are so important, however, that they may defeat the finest army that was ever led to battle, and so I say that unless conscription is effective in respect to these agencies our preparation is a useless waste of money, and indeed, is an added incentive to getting us into trouble.
We maintain the nucleus of an armed force so that we may be able to build up in time of emergency a force for the defence of the state. We maintain military experts capable of handling men for that purpose, but to whom have we entrusted the handling of the industries of the country in time of war? To whom have we entrusted the handling of the finances of the country in time of war? These are left to whoever may be on the job, and they are left as profit making agencies for private individuals, whereas, on the other hand, we conscript our men to do the fighting.
For efficiency in defence the entire resources of the nation must be mobilized. We now rely upon our ability to lure industry by war time prices to do service to the state. We rely upon our ability to lure finance by offering the nation as a bond slave for all time in order to get financial institutions to perform their function in time of national danger. It is not sufficient to trust to these allurements. Indeed, we can no longer put our faith in them. Patriotic speeches during the last great war pledged with fervour the last man and the last dollar, but if you add up the ledger of the nation after the last war you will find that while we were many thousands of men short, we were, or somebody was, many millions of dollars ahead. The last dollar-nay, even the first one-never was given, but the last man was ready to go.
I submit that a democratic country must rise to its own defence with every citizen on a democratic footing. Let us think for a
moment of the injustice of the present practice. We conscript men to die, or worse, we conscript them to be crippled in conflict in the national interests, but we leave others free to grow rich on what has been well termed blood money. Now I contend before this parliament to-day that bankers, captains of industry, merchants, railway companies, and so forth, should be put on the same footing as soldiers in the matter of national service during war. Let their pay be the same, let them be under the same discipline, let them be subject to the same restrictions and to the same punishments as the soldier. Let the banker who fails to do his duty during war time be put against a wall and shot at dawn, just as the soldier is who refuses to do his duty.
The effect of this arrangement on the morale of the nation would contribute more to efficiency than do large expenditures on military preparations. Morale has become a very essential factor in war success. During the great war it was found that the morale of the belligerent nations had to be maintained at any cost, and at times in order to maintain that morale appeals weTe made to the lowest elements of human nature. At times, even lies were used freely in all countries to preserve that thing called morale. Now, could anything be more disrupting than the thought that while many are dying for their country, others are becoming rich by profiteering in the things that are essential to the national life. Could there be anything more calculated to unify a people, raise their morale, and bring them into one strong, fighting force than for everyone to know that no one was making blood money out of the conflict? More serious to contemplate is the possibility that the time is not far distant when young men will rather be shot at home than be shot in the front line as a protest against their country being so unjust and unthinking as to conscript its youth to fight while it leaves the privileged few to profit out of the calamity of the nation.
But there is a graver aspect to this question than even its injustice and its detrimental effect on the morale of the people. While a man will fight to the death against considerable odds for his country, finance in the hands of private bankers on an interest-bearing basis will quit at the first sight of danger to itself. There is a well-defined point beyond which finance will not go, but will turn like a traitor and run for cover. Finance will quit, no matter what position the nation may be in, just so soon as the national debt reaches the highest amount at which it will be considered by bankers possible to extract the interest

National Service-Mr. Irvine
in the form of taxation from generations to come. At that . point, no matter how the nation may be situated finance will take cover. The nation may be in a struggle for its very existence, and a few more weeks or months may cany it to victory, but even under such dire circumstances if those in control of finance discover that finance is in danger, the victory of the nation will be sacrificed. That is the position we are in at the present time. If under the present system national safety in war should clash with financial safety, the latter will win.
Conscription in war time of the various agencies referred to in the resolution would of course increase production by preventing duplication and overlapping, which are inevitable under the competitive system. It would1 also eliminate all the waste of labour and material so common in times of peace, and would conserve the resources of the state to the utmost during the conflict.
Let me submit also, Mr. Speaker, that this is the right time to make provision for the proper conduct of the next war, because if war ever comes upon us again we want to be ready. We do not wish to have to make all these regulations when the country is in the midst of the struggle. We ought to make them now. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) should be acquainted with the entire industrial organization of the state. He should know exactly where to put his finger, and when, and he should have it so organized that at a moment's notice he could bring every agency in the state to its defence. That cannot be done whale we go on in the haphazard way in which we have been going in the past. He has no authority to do that. He himself has not had the training which he should have in the overlooking of these industries while such supervision is not considered to be part of our protective program. But not only so, it will not be easy for the minister of national defence, whoever he' may be when the next war comes-of course, we are always hoping that another war will never come-but it will not be easy, I say, for the minister of national defence at that time to make the alteration which I seek now, because when the music of the shekels as they jingle into the coffers of profiteers, accelerated as they will be by war demands, begins to fall upon the ears of the privileged, he will find it very difficult to alter the regulations. He will be met then with the excuse: Let things alone as they are; don't disrupt industry while war is going on; and so forth and so on. This, then, is the time for us to act. Let every industrial magnate and every financier in this country be told 
that if war ever comes to Canada again everything will be conscripted for national defence, no profit will be permitted. Let us do that now by legislation.
I come to the elaboration of my next point, and that is, to conscript the agencies required for war purposes described in the resolution would be the best and the most effective assurance of lasting peace that we could have. If what my resolution proposes, namely, automatic conscription in war time of every agency employed in national defence, were put into effect, then we would be absolutely certain of two things of great importance. First, that we were fully prepared, or at least that we were prepared to the utmost extent of the nation's resources. If justified in making any preparation at all, it is, as I have pointed out, our patriotic duty to be fully prepared. There can be no adequate excuse for a partial preparation if there be any reason for preparation at all. Underlying our present policy is the fear, well founded, of a possible war in which we may be called upon to defend ourselves. That well-founded fear compels us to make certain preparations for our defence, and no one can say, if the fear is well founded, that we should be content with anything short of the utmost preparation. I say, let us prepare adequately or stop spending public money in what would be little short of a farce were we really launched into a conflict. The conscription of all natural resources and essential services, including transportation facilities, industrial plants, and commercial and financial agencies, would be adequate preparation at no additional cost, and it would mean, as I say, that we would know for a certainly that if war did come we would have all the resources of the country behind us in the struggle, and that we would all be on a democratic footing.
But the second thing which would be made certain were the course followed which I have proposed is that if war did come under these circumstances, everyone would know that the war was inevitable. That is to say, that it had not been fostered by some private interests for private gain. The war lords then would not be tempted to plunge the country into a death struggle for the sake of profit. Thus this sort of preparation which I suggest would be of real assistance to lasting peace. It has long been the claim of militarists that preparation is the best guarantee of peace. That has proven to be false in the past because preparation was confined to the manufacture of munitions and the training of armies. That sort of preparation has proven to be an added incentive to conflict. But if our preparation extend to all the profit-making agencies

National Service-Mr. Irvine
esseutiai to the winning of a war, then indeed it would be true that such preparation would be our best safeguard against war. I do not doubt for a moment the general belief that past wars have been urged and promoted by individuals and corporations having great influence on international policy and standing to profit by war.
Of all the dark and despicable suspicions that could becloud the consciousness of a nation this is the worst. To what low levels of bestial materialism has the desire for profit brought mankind 1-if it be true that there are men in every nation who will not hesitate to plunge their fellows into the shambles of war for the sake of trade and profit for themselves. Some hon. members may have doubts about the truth of this charge. I will not stop to bring the proofs, first, because it is not essential to my argument, and secondly because it were better not to demonstrate this repulsive deformity of the human imagination. Whether it be true or not that men have promoted wars for profit, no one will deny that individuals do profit greatly by wars. That being so, it is very unwise to trust frail human nature to such great temptation. The government is asked now to pass the resolution before the house in order that the nation may be freed from the danger of war at the instigation of profiteers, and that the minds of the people may be freed from the dark fears and suspicions they entertain in this regard.
I emphasize the second step in my argument: that to make provision for the conscription of the agencies mentioned in the resolution would afford adequate preparation for defence at no additional cost; that, since the preparations that are now made are made because of our fear of possible attack, it is illogical to stop short of adequate preparation-and the proposal I make would be adequate; and that this sort of preparation would be the best assurance of peace, in that it would do away with the profit incentive which is alleged to be a dangerous cause of war. This profit incentive, being a danger, should be removed especially since such action would bring tranquility to the public mind, now disturbed by the suspicion which falls on our money kings and captains of industry.
I turn now to another step in the argument, namely, that under the proposed conscription measure war would be possible without war debt, or at the worst the nation would owe the amount of war debt to itself. The last war was financed largely through the treasury board. The national treasury or national credit was the source, the Finance Act the means, and the banks were the agents in the
transaction. But when the war was over the nation owed the banks the entire amount expended in the war. The only reason why this entire transaction did not result in dire calamity through the revolt of the people was, I think, that the people generally did not understand what had actually been done. Under the resolution the next war-if by any misfortune it should come-would be financed from the same source as the last-only, when it is all over, we shall not owe the amount a second time, with interest, to a few privileged financiers.
For clarity on this point I shall use a simple illustration. Let us suppose a war between two tribes in the days of tribal society. To make it simple we will suppose that these tribes fought with rocks. When they went to war with each other they naturally organized themselves for the struggle. The young men went to the front line to throw the rocks, a number of others were selected to gather rocks and carry them to the front, and a third group were selected to do the hunting and to prepare the food for the entire tribe during the period of the war. But when the war was over it was found that nobody owed anybody else; everyone in the tribe had done his part: all the rocks had been gathered and did not have to be paid for and the tribe was as free of debt as it was the day it began fighting. That is not so to-day, however. We have, of course, complications arising from different methods of warfare, but the principle is precisely the same. In the last war there were in Canada men who neither gathered rocks nor threw them, but when the war was over we had to pay them for eveTy rock that was gathered and thrown. And generations to come will be unable to pay that debt. It is indeed questionable whether, when we add the accumulating interest bo the national debt growing out of the last war, the debt will ever be paid off. We should prepare now so that in the next war we might be able to finance it without paying interest to anyone. The nation in that case would owe its debt to itself.
I want to leave this thought with the Minister of National Defence, and so that he may be able to express his opinion on it before six o'clock I will now close, contenting myself with pointing out that, if carried into effect, this resolution will make war very unlikely in the future for the reason that the profit incentive will have been removed. But if war should occur notwithstanding, then we shall be prepared to put to our defence the entire resources of the nation, and no one will make any profit at
