speechtext:
I will not take more
than a few minutes to discuss the motion. As a matter of fact, I did not know that the resolution would foe reached this afternoon and therefore I shall be unable to deal as exhaustively as I might with the arguments my hon. friend (Mr. Irvine) has put forward. I want the hon. gentleman to feel, however, that if my observations are brief it is not because I do not realize the full importance of the subject he has discussed, or the very able and temperate manner in which he has advanced his arguments. I think the house and the country are indebted to the hon. gentleman for the way in which he has stated his case.
In countries where recruiting is voluntary, the suggestion which the hon. member has made regarding national mobilization is perhaps more ideal than practical; and I note that he has recognized that fact inasmuch as, in the very teeth of his resolution, is the proviso that conscription be effective in relation to man power. The policy he advocates, with the proviso which is added, is one which, in my opinion at least, will find acceptance in a general way; that is to say, that men should not be conscripted to give their lives in war while) the industrial resources of the country are allowed to go free without making their just contribution. I believe we all accept that principle. Perhaps my hon. friend does not know that it is a part of the responsibility of a minister occupying the position which I hold-much as he may deprecate, as I do, the idea of any possible conflict in the future-to consider plans for industrial mobilization in the event of such a conflict arising. That is the principle adopted in Great Britain; the Imperial defence committee has been engaged in a consideration of it. We in this country are in touch with the proceedings of that committee and the principle is not by any means new to a proper administration of the defence department. I feel that the principles which the hon. member has enunciated can best be carried out by an endeavour, in time of peace, to work out a policy of industrial mobilization which will take into proper account the utilization of all the forces of the nation and not simply of man power alone. We will see to it that every part of the nation, industry, finance, labour and transportation, all make their just contributions towards carrying on the conflict if such turns out to be inevitable. I hope 
what I say now may perhaps lead my hon. friend to not press this resolution for acceptance by this house, since he has had the opportunity of discussing this matter; I want to say to him that I do feel as Minister of National Defence, and also as a minister who has something to do with the peace of the country, that it would be a mistake for us at this time to pass a resolution which seems to me to indicate to the world at large that we are thinking about war. My hon. friend's resolution provides that in the opinion of this house it is advisable that legislation be enacted providing that upon the declaration of war involving Canada, all natural resources and so on shall become conscripted automatically. I do feel that this will be misunderstood by the countries of the world, if we now make a legislative declaration that we are preparing for war even in this way.
We have on the order paper to-day no less than two resolutions advocating peace and looking to the eventual consummation of world peace. One resolution is proposed by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), who suggests that this matter is so important that a special department should be created having to do with peace and international understanding. There is another resolution proposed by an hon. member of this house which suggests that Canada should become a party to the optional clause respecting the world court. Both these resolutions are absolutely apposed to the resolution now before the house, and while in general terms I believe the principle of the resolution will be accepted if the proviso concerning conscription is also accepted, I do suggest to my hon. friend that having had the benefit of this discussion, it would be a mistake at this time to pass this resolution. I believe sincerely that we would be regarded as advertising that this country is preparing for war, just at the very time when all endeavours are being made in the direction of peace. We had the Washington conference last September; we have the Preparatory commission meeting again with regard to disarmament, and perhaps more machinery than ever is being set up in an endeavour to solve this age-old question of whether the peoples of the world cannot live together in peace.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSCRIPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND ESSENTIAL SERVICES IN TIME OF WAR

Some of us find ourselves in rather an awkward predicament with regard to this resolution. It seems odd that those who have stood very firmly for peace find themselves rather inclined to sympathize with the resolution, while the Minister of National Defence has placed himself in very strong opposition to it, on the ground that it may be misunderstood abroad and may not accomplish anything in the direction of peace. I think none of us will doubt the sincerity of the minister when he advocates peace, but I am not so sure of his consistency; I have no doubt he believes himself consistent, but I am not quite so sure that his position is in reality consistent. He says that the industrial resources of the country should make their "just contribution" in the event of war. That is all very well as a general statement, but I should like to ask whether, after having passed through a great war, the industrial forces and equipment of this country can be said to have made their just contribution.
What is a just contribution? I know that to-day a committee is sitting to consider soldiers' pensions; I know that many pitiable cases have come before that committee. Men are living on the very verge of poverty, some of them precluded from government assistance, and it would seem to me, in view of the finances of the country, that the government is prepared to assist these men only in the most grudging fashion. That is true, but on the other hand surely we know that the great part of the load of taxation we are bearing at present, and which perhaps more than anything else prevents the expansion of industry and the entry of new people into this country, is very largely the result of the last war. Do we not alii recognize the fact, as the Minister of Finance recently informed us, that 50 per cent of the total expenditures of this country are to pay for the last war or are in connection with the present military expenditures? As I pointed out on another occasion, if we add to that the increased expenditure involved in securing our greatly increased income and the increased expenditure in connection with additional financing, altogether expenditure due to war amounts to about two-thirds of our total national expenditure. That is the situation we must face to-day.
The other day an appeal was made to this house by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Smoke) suggesting that we in this generation should bear the burden of ithe past war and not pass it on to future generations. What was the response to that suggestion? There was none whatever. We are finding that although a great many people made fortunes during the war, even at this early stage the government are repudiating the income tax, which was levied to pay for the war, and so those who made fortunes either directly out of the war or indirectly because of the war, those who are the wealthy people of to-day, are going free to a very large extent. On the other hand, the people who are asked to pay for the war are the ordinary people who paid over and over again even during the progress of that war.
Is it fair to say that in any future war we should insist that industry and finance should make their just contributions unless we at this time insist that industry and finance do that today with regard to the last war? I think I would say that the minister would be consistent if he would introduce, or have the government introduce, a measure at this session asking that the last war should be paid for by a levy on industry and finance to-day. The people engaged in industry and finance are the only people in this country who benefited because of the war.
The minister says that he is quite sincere in urging that it would be a mistake for this house to pass the resolution, that it might be misunderstood. I recognize that possibly there is a danger along that line, but I would suggest that the nations of the world are not ignorant of the situation in Canada. They know perfectly well that we are spending today some-what is it?-$18,000,000 upon military defence, and that within the past few years we have gone up almost 50 per cent in our military expenditures. I would say that if the minister is as consistent as I sincerely

believe he thinks himself/ he would reduce even the present comparatively small expenditure on armaments. That would be the very best declaration to the world that Canada is pacific in her intentions.
I should like to examine for a moment the terms of the resolution:
Whereas, it is the existent policy of this country that reasonable preparation should be made for self-defence in case of any war involving Canada.
Is that true? I think we must admit that it is. If any of us come here and suggest that we have national disarmament-a policy of which I personally am in favour, one of the policies on which I was elected to this house, a policy that I find is endorsed by a large number of labour organizations, farm organizations and church organizations across this country, and which is backed up by a very large number of returned men who know what war really is-I say that if we suggest that we should have a policy of national disarmament we are told immediately that that is impracticable, in fact, at least in some quarters, we are told that we are unpatriotic to suggest that. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the time is coming before so very long when hon. gentlemen in this house will get credit for absolute sincerity in this matter, and it will be admitted that those of us who advocate disarmament may be just as sincere in our position, and just as patriotic, as, on the other hand, I believe those are who advocate armaments. I do not think that the people who want armies, and navies, and air forces are consciously unpatriotic. But from my standpoint I believe that they are doing everything they can to ruin my country; and believing that from the bottom of my heart, and having taken that stand in the past, I, as a member of this house, who is trying to represent the people of the country, am bound to say so. I do not believe that expenditure on armament is the way to increase the prosperity of Canada, I do not believe that it is the way to effect the security of Canada or the security of the world. There are better ways, and it seems to me that we ought not to be labelled unpatriotic when we sincerely believe that, state that position, and try to impress our views upon the country.

No, it is another matter. I do not want to be diverted from this argument. I wish to go on with the latter part of the resolution which states:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is advisable that .legislation be enacted providing that on the declaration of war involving Canada, all natural resources and essential services, including transportation facilities, industrial plants and commercial and financial agencies, should automatically be conscripted for national service for the duration of the war.
Can we imagine that if that proposal were actually in force in Canada, we would be liable to go into another war? I take it that such legislation would be one of the greatest deterrents against war that it would be possible to have. Just fancy if all the capital in all the banks were immediately conscripted and if the banks, instead of being able to make money out of the war as they did before, knew that it would annihilate them, do you think there is a banker in this country or in Europe who would consent to war? If it means that all our railway systems would immediately be conscripted, do you think that the leaders of the great transportation systems in this country would submit? If it means that all the industrial plants would immediately be conscripted and every man rendered penniless, reduced to the position of the conscripted soldier at $1.10 a day, would any man in Canada be likely under those circumstances to be in favour of war? I would urge that, if that were the situation, immediately any suggestion of war arose from one end of the country to the other the leaders of all the great newspapers, the men on the boards of all our great universities, the men who to a certain extent influence the policies of all our institutions, would set in operation such a campaign of education, such a protest against war, that the very appearance of war would be swept away and we would immediately resort to some pacific method of settling our disputes.

speechtext: I should like to ask the peaceful member for Winnipeg North Centre how he would handle a peaceful strike such as they had in Winnipeg a few years ago, and how he would be able to procure milk for the babies if we did not have some troops in Canada.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSCRIPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND ESSENTIAL SERVICES IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext:
I think hon. members will quite agree that when anyone is driven to such desperate means to try to sidetrack one in an argument, his case is pretty nearly hopeless. During the big strike

my policy, for which I have no reason to feel ashamed, was that of peace. It was then and it is to-day.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSCRIPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND ESSENTIAL SERVICES IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext: A peaceful strike.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSCRIPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND ESSENTIAL SERVICES IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext: Yes, if men want to stop work, unless they are to be degraded to the position of veritable slaves they have a right to do so-at least until we are able to arrange other means -which, I hope, may be forthcoming so that these difficulties which now arise in the industrial world wall not precipitate us into the unfortunate strikes which sometimes we have. But force, brute force, may I call it?-and I know all my comrades in the industrial world do not agree with this, but I take this position and more among the labour people believe in it than among the captains of industry-is absolutely no solution of our industrial problems. I do not believe it is any solution of our economic problems or of our international problems. This method of war is an outgrown method. In the old days our ancestors got down into the slime and fought with their teeth and fists; we think that we have reached another stage than that. In our ordinary business and social life we have reached the stage when, if we have a dispute, we refer it to the courts, to atbitration; we settle it in some other way than by force. Surely we might hope that in our international questions we may advance along similar lines. Progress is everywhere to be found. The League of Nations Society is now uiging the establishment of those institutions and policies which will prevent international complications. We from our comer have introduced some resolutions along that line, and I trust that the hon. gentlemen who have done me the honour to interrupt to-day will vote in favour of the resolution of my colleague, and that we shall make representations to Great Britain along the line of signing the optional clause of the Peace treaty. If we do that as a country we shall have advanced a long way, but in the meantime, believing as I do, that war is an obsolete and inefficient instrument for the maintenance of peace-

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSCRIPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND ESSENTIAL SERVICES IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext: Everybody agrees with that.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSCRIPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND ESSENTIAL SERVICES IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext:
Very good but so long as Canada is committed, as the minister of National Defence states, to armaments in order to attain her ends, I cannot see how any of us can fail, in carrying out that policy of armament and militarism, to say that if we go to the point where we conscript men, we ought to go the whole way. Surely men are worth more than property; if we conscript men, I urge in the name of all the returned

Private Bills
men. who have served at the front and of all of those who have sacrificed, let us go the whole way and insist that when the next war cranes we shall all suffer equally.

speechtext: I should just like to say as a returned man that I refuse to allow the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) to speak for me.
